extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, classical philosophy, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and summarise Plato's criteria for judging poetry, poets, and the moral/educational effects of art as presented in Books IX–X of the Republic, and the commentary's counter-arguments about art's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of pleasures: reason versus sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato contrasts the 'pleasures of reason' (intellectual, at rest) with fleeting 'sensual pleasures' and emotions, preferring the former as superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He distinguishes necessary and unnecessary pleasures and a further class of 'wild beast' pleasures; notes intellectual pleasures are more elevating but not necessarily more lasting and depend on bodily state. Use this criterion to judge whether a pleasure (or aesthetic experience) cultivates reason or merely satisfies transient senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical/figurative measure of moral difference (the 729 interval)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato uses a numerical/arithmetic formula (the cube of 9 = 729) as a metaphor to express the vast interval separating the kingly life from the tyrannical life and their respective pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a philosophical/figurative device for indicating immeasurable moral difference; the commentary notes the use of geometric/arithmetic form as giving apparent verification. Consider such formal devices as rhetorical means to quantify moral or aesthetic distances rather than literal metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is thrice removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (and painter) is an imitator 'thrice removed from the king and from the truth': God (form) → craftsman → painter → poet, so the poet's work is an imitation of an imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this as a critique of artistic truthfulness: poetry deals in appearances, not first principles. Examples in the text (bed made by God, carpenter, painter) illustrate the degrees of removal. Use this to question a work's epistemic relation to reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets lack knowledge; they depict appearances, not true art or use
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation 'is devoid of knowledge, being only a kind of play or sport'; poets can describe arts without possessing the practical or theoretical knowledge those arts require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's skill in representation does not substitute for understanding the subject depicted (e.g., a poet can 'delineate any art' without knowing its use). Treat claims that art educates or imparts expertise with scepticism unless demonstrable knowledge is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry addresses inferior parts of the soul and enfeebles reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'concerned with an inferior part of the soul. He indulges the feelings, while he enfeebles the reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art by which faculties it engages: if it mainly excites passions and undermines the rational faculties that measure 'greater and less', it is judged harmful. This is a normative test for the social/political suitability of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry injures by exciting sympathy and unhealthy imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'heaviest count' is that poetry injuriously excites the feelings: sympathy with on-stage sorrow or buffoonery leads to indulgence of those feelings and may make us act in ways we otherwise condemn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples given—weeping at another's sorrows leading to self-weeping; laughing at buffoonery turning one into a buffoon—to flag anti-patterns: works that stimulate maladaptive emotional imitation are to be restricted or censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible poetry must be useful as well as delightful
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be allowed to return only if it 'can show that she is useful as well as delightful'; otherwise love of poetry must be renounced despite its charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a dual test for allowing art in the ideal state: demonstrable usefulness (ethical/educational) plus aesthetic delight. The text suggests limiting acceptable poetry to 'hymns to the Gods and praises of famous men' and requires poets (or their supporters) to defend usefulness—an explicit policy criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor/performer profession degrades character
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato regards the profession of an actor as degrading because 'one man in his life cannot play many parts'—the characters an actor performs seem to destroy his own character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge performance-based arts by their effects on the performer's identity and character formation; if role-playing undermines authenticity or moral firmness, it is morally suspect according to this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets are not reliable educators or lawmakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates interrogates Homer: did Homer give laws, lead wars, found ways of life? The absence of such practical influence is used to argue poets are not effective educators of a polis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical/social efficacy as a test: if a purported educator (poet) has not actually guided public life or produced followers who organize society around their teachings, question their claim to be a moral or political guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's potential to ennoble and express the ideal (counter-argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter to Plato: 'art is not merely imitation, but rather the expression of the ideal in forms of sense'—artists can ennoble humble subjects and convey ideals (examples: Rembrandt, Turner, Pheidias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a positive evaluative criterion for art: whether it conveys an ideal, elevates mundane subject-matter, or embodies a 'visible embodiment of the divine.' Works that do so rebut Plato's wholesale rejection of poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as catharsis versus indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato rejects Aristotle's catharsis (that tragedy purges pity and fear), seeing imitation as affording indulgence of the passions; the commentary allows that some expressions of emotion can harmonize or heal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to assess tragic art: determine whether a work produces constructive emotional resolution (purging, harmonizing) or merely stimulates unhealthy indulgence. The therapeutic value of art is a key evaluative axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should train choice amidst life's mixtures (lesson from Er)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the myth of Er: 'education should be directed to the acquisition of such a knowledge as will teach a man to refuse the evil and choose the good'—teaching people to choose by reference to the nature of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pedagogical aims of art and education by whether they cultivate judgment to navigate life’s mixed combinations (beauty with poverty/wealth, knowledge with external goods) and to prefer the life that makes men better rather than merely happier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards of justice and the immortality narrative as moral inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: The tale of Er provides graphic rewards/punishments and a cosmology where justice is ultimately rewarded: souls are judged, choose lives, drink from the river of Forgetfulness, and are reborn according to choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mythic or narrative representations of justice and afterlife as instruments in moral education: their clarity, vividness, and motivational force are criteria for their usefulness in promoting just behaviour.
